en: Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya Ariṣṭanemi grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati grant us well-being.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Oṃ.
Then Āśvalāyana, having approached the Blessed One Parameṣṭhin, spoke to him.
"Teach me, O Blessed One, the most excellent knowledge of Brahman, which is ever practiced by the virtuous and remains hidden;
by which, having quickly cast off all evil, the wise man attains the Puruṣa who is higher than the highest. (1)
To him the Grandfather said: "Learn it through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation;
not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality. (2)

Beyond the sky, that which is placed in the secret cave shines forth, which the ascetics enter—those ascetics whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of the Vedānta, who are pure in being by virtue of the yoga of renunciation. //3//
In the worlds of Brahmā, at the time of the ultimate end, they shall all be completely liberated through supreme immortality;
and one who is pure, seated on a comfortable seat in a secluded place, with neck, head, and body held straight. //4//

Abiding in the final stage of life, having restrained all the senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru, he should contemplate the stainless and pure lotus of the heart as being luminous, serene, and free from sorrow in its center. //5//

Inconceivable, unmanifest, of infinite forms, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman—him who is without beginning, middle, or end, the one, all-pervading, formless wonder of consciousness and bliss. //6//

Having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, who has Umā as his companion, the three-eyed one, the blue-throated, the profoundly tranquil, the sage goes to that source of all beings, the witness of all, who stands beyond darkness. (7)
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra; he is the imperishable, supreme self-ruler.
He alone is Viṣṇu, he is the vital breath, he is time, fire, and the moon. //8//
He alone is everything that has been and all that is to be, the eternal;
knowing Him, one transcends death—there is no other path to liberation. //9//
Perceiving the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self, one attains the supreme Brahman; not by any other means. //10//
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, the wise man burns away his evil through the practice of churning with knowledge. //11//
That very self, its nature deluded by māyā, assumes a body and performs all actions;
through various enjoyments such as women, food, and drink, it attains complete satisfaction while awake. //12//

In the dream state, that living being (jīva), the enjoyer of pleasure and pain within the world of living beings fashioned by its own māyā, enters into a state of bliss when all [mental faculties] have dissolved during deep sleep and it is overcome by darkness (tamas). //13//
Furthermore, through the connection with the karma of other births, that very same living being sleeps and then awakens;
that living being who sports within the three cities is from whom all this diverse universe is born. //14//
In that [state] which is sustaining bliss and indivisible awakening, the three cities also dissolve. //14*//
From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which sustains the universe. 15.
That which is the supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe, subtler than the subtle and eternal—that you alone are; you alone are that. 16.
Having realized that "I am that Brahman," which illumines the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, one is liberated from all bonds. //17//
Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes—I am the witness distinct from these, pure consciousness alone, eternally auspicious. //18//
Everything has arisen in me alone; everything is established in me;
everything goes to dissolution in me; therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman. //19//
Thus ends the first section.
I alone am subtler than the subtlest; likewise, I am the Great One. I am the manifold universe.
I am the Ancient One, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord; I am the Golden One, I am the form of Śiva. //20//
I am without hands or feet, yet possessed of inconceivable power; I see without eyes and hear without ears.
I know all things while remaining of a solitary nature, and there is no knower of me; I am eternally consciousness itself. //21//
By many Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
For me there is neither merit nor sin, no destruction, and no birth; I possess no body, senses, or intellect. 22.
There is no earth, no water, nor fire; there is no wind for me, nor is there space.
Having thus known the form of the Supreme Self—dwelling in the cave of the heart, partless and non-dual—[one is liberated]. //23//
One attains the pure form of the Supreme Self, the witness of all, which is devoid of both existence and non-existence. //23*//

Whoever studies the Śatarudrīya becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind; he becomes purified by the self; he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor; he becomes purified from the killing of a Brahmin; he becomes purified from the theft of gold;

he becomes purified from [the consequences of] what should and should not be done. Therefore, one who has taken refuge in Avimukta—whether belonging to an [ascetic] order or not—should recite it always or even once.
By this, one attains the knowledge that destroys the ocean of saṃsāra;
therefore, having understood it thus, one enjoys the state (fruit) of absolute liberation.
One enjoys the state (fruit) of absolute liberation. //24//
Thus ends the Kaivalya Upanishad in the Atharvaveda.
Oṃ tat sat.
